name: Odell Purdy
languages: Spanish (vaquero Spanish, from the Nueces brush country)
equipment: Leather duster, sun-faded to the colour of dust, over a red flannel shirt, batwing chaps and a vest with a tally book in the pocket
Navy revolver (Colt 1851, converted to cartridge, his since the first drive in 1869), 6 loaded
Lariat, sixty feet of braided rawhide, and a short piggin string
Saddle, bridle, spurs with Mexican rowels, a saddle blanket and saddle bags
A DA&P stock agent's card: in charge of the railroad's horse herd and the twelve head going out in the stock car on Saturday
A harmonica, a hoof pick, a pocket of horehound candy for the horses, and a tobacco sack of coffee beans for himself
Horse: Deacon, a grulla gelding with a black stripe down his back and an opinion about everything
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; once per long rest he shrugs off a level of trail exhaustion; his rations last a day longer than anyone else's)

Saddle-Born (Cowhand: advantage on Riding checks, no disadvantage on ranged attacks from the saddle, mounts or dismounts with 5 ft of movement. Deacon is part of him: Deacon has extra hit points equal to 5 x his cowhand level, never spooks under him, comes to his whistle from half a mile and acts on his initiative. Lariat: proficient, and from the saddle he throws a loop as a bonus action)
Rawhide (Cowhand: advantage on saves against exhaustion, heat and cold; he rides 12 hours a day without forced-march saves and spends one extra Hit Die on a short rest)
Cow Sense (Cowhand, 2nd level: advantage on Animal Handling with cattle, horses and mules; he turns a stampede's leaders with one check as an action, with advantage)

Outfit: Vaquero (Cowhand, 3rd level: the roping tradition he learned from Tejano vaqueros on the Nueces; his lariat reaches 40 ft, a creature he ropes from the saddle can be thrown prone and dragged without a further check, and he can rope two targets at once)

The Trail Outfit (Cattle Drover background: every trail hand, ranch cook and cattle buyer from the Nueces to the Platte knows somebody who rode with Odell Purdy, and will give him a meal, a remount or the truth)

personality.traits: I am easy-going and slow to anger, and I like to tell a long story slowly. I talk to horses more than people, and I trust their opinions more.
personality.ideals: A man is what he does when the herd runs. Talk is cheap; nighthawking in a hailstorm is not.
personality.bonds: Deacon. My mother, Lettie, who runs a laundry in Fort Worth and writes me every month in a hand she learned at forty. And every man I ever rode drag with, black, white or Mexican, who ate my dust and shared his coffee.
personality.flaws: I let people underestimate me because it is easier, and sometimes I let them for too long. And I will not leave a horse behind, not for anything.

appearance: A broad-shouldered, easy-moving Black man of twenty-seven with a wide good-humoured face, a thin moustache, a scar across the back of his right hand from a rope burn, and a battered tan hat with a rattlesnake band. He walks bow-legged and looks most comfortable leaning on a fence.
backstory: Odell Purdy was born enslaved on a cotton farm near Waco, Texas, in 1852, and was thirteen when freedom came. He went to work for a cattleman on the Nueces at fourteen, learned the trade from Tejano vaqueros who taught him the rope, the language and the saddle, and rode his first drive up the Chisholm Trail to Abilene in 1869. He made six drives in eight years, wrangler, then point rider, then trail boss's right hand, and in 1878 he came up the Goodnight country to Colorado with a herd and decided he liked the mountains. The DA&P hired him to buy, break and keep the horses for its construction crews. On Saturday he is shipping twelve head over the pass in the stock car of the first through train, for the track gangs at Hollowell Junction, and he is riding with them because Deacon is going too and Deacon does not ride with strangers. Mrs. Ruane asked him to keep his carbine handy. He said he always does.
